text: The ISRO mission statement articulates the organisation's fundamental purpose: to harness space technology for national development while pursuing space science research and planetary exploration. ISRO's activities are organised into three major programme areas: space applications, space science, and launch vehicle technology. The space applications programme focuses on communication satellites, Earth observation satellites, and satellite-based navigation systems. The space science programme conducts research in astronomy, astrophysics, planetary science, and space weather. The launch vehicle programme develops rockets for placing Indian satellites in orbit. All three programmes are supported by a strong infrastructure of research centres, test facilities, and ground stations.

The Indian Space Programme's Sarabhai Profile represents a comprehensive twenty-year roadmap for India's space capabilities. Phase I (1969-1975) focuses on sounding rockets, the first satellite (Aryabhata), and the SITE experiment. Phase II (1975-1980) envisions the development of the SLV and the first operational communication satellite. Phase III (1980-1990) projects the development of larger launch vehicles (ASLV, PSLV) and a constellation of operational satellites for communication, meteorology, and remote sensing. This phased approach ensures that each achievement builds upon the last, creating an ascending spiral of capability and confidence.

The Physical Research Laboratory's contributions to Indian science extend far beyond its original mandate of cosmic ray research. Over two decades, PRL has pioneered research in space physics, astronomy, planetary science, geosciences, and theoretical physics. The laboratory has trained hundreds of scientists who now work across India's scientific establishment — at ISRO, the Department of Atomic Energy, universities, and other research institutions. PRL's alumni network is one of the most powerful in Indian science, creating a web of relationships and shared values that strengthens the entire national scientific enterprise.

ATIRA's operational methodology demonstrates how research institutions can serve industry effectively. The association's research programme is driven by the needs of its member mills, who pay annual subscriptions and in return receive access to research results, technical advisory services, testing facilities, and training programmes. This demand-driven model ensures that ATIRA's research is relevant and immediately applicable. At the same time, ATIRA maintains a programme of longer-term strategic research that anticipates future industry challenges. The balance between responsive service and forward-looking research is one of the keys to ATIRA's success and a model that other industry research associations in India are now emulating.

The Sarabhai approach to institution building can be distilled into five principles. First, clarity of purpose: every institution must have a clear, compelling mission that everyone in the organisation understands and believes in. Second, excellence in people: recruit the best talent, give them extraordinary freedom and responsibility, and hold them to the highest standards. Third, strategic partnerships: collaborate with the best institutions in the world, not as a supplicant but as a peer. Fourth, financial sustainability: design the institution's funding model to ensure long-term viability without excessive dependence on any single source. Fifth, organic growth: start small, prove the concept, and expand gradually as capabilities mature.
source: Analysis of Sarabhai's Institution Building Philosophy, IIMA Case Study, 1970

text: The IIM Ahmedabad Board of Governors, under the chairmanship of Dr. Vikram Sarabhai, has approved a strategic plan that positions the institute as a centre of excellence in management education and research for the developing world. The plan calls for the development of academic programmes tailored to the needs of Indian industry and public administration, the establishment of research centres in areas such as agricultural management, public systems, and technology management, and the creation of executive education programmes for practicing managers. The plan also emphasises the importance of developing indigenous teaching materials — case studies drawn from Indian organisations — to replace the predominantly American case studies currently in use.
